title: India rejects US court's bid to serve Pannun lawsuit papers on NSA Doval via Delhi courts
dek: A New York judge has asked three Delhi courts to deliver the papers after India refused service under the Hague Convention. The MEA called the lawsuit baseless.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
India on Friday rejected an attempt by a court in New York to deliver summonses in a civil lawsuit to National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and former Research and Analysis Wing (RAW) chief Samant Goel through courts in Delhi. "We reject such baseless lawsuits," the Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson, Randhir Jaiswal, said at the ministry's weekly briefing, according to reports.

The lawsuit was filed by Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, the founder of the banned group Sikhs for Justice, who is wanted in India on terrorism charges and holds US and Canadian citizenship. He is seeking damages over what he says was a plot to kill him in New York, and accuses Mr Doval of directing it with the involvement of RAW, India's external intelligence agency. The US government is not a party to the case.

## What the court ordered

In an order dated 13 November, Judge Katherine Polk Failla of the US District Court for the Southern District of New York directed the court clerk to send the papers through three Delhi courts: the Patiala House district court for Mr Doval, and the Dwarka and Tis Hazari courts for Mr Goel, according to reports. "The court respectfully requests the assistance of receiving Indian courts in effecting service of process," the order says, according to reports.

The judge said the court's first attempt to serve the documents through India's designated central authority under the Hague Service Convention, the treaty that governs how court papers are delivered across borders, had been rejected. She allowed an alternative method under Article 19 of the convention and provisions of India's Code of Civil Procedure, reports said. The papers were passed to the Indian Embassy in Washington with a diplomatic note from the State Department, which said the step did not reflect any US position on the case, according to reports.

## India's position

When the issue came up earlier this month, on 10 November, Mr Jaiswal called the allegations "fabricated and malicious" and said requests to serve foreign judicial documents in India could only be routed through the Ministry of Law and Justice, according to reports. Indian officials described the court's latest step as routine and procedural and said the summonses were not binding, according to reports citing unnamed officials.

An earlier attempt to serve Mr Doval in person, when he accompanied Prime Minister Narendra Modi to the United States in February, failed; the court later found he had not been served, according to reports.

## Background

The civil case is separate from a criminal case in New York in which US prosecutors have charged an Indian national, Nikhil Gupta, and a former Indian intelligence officer, Vikash Yadav, over an alleged murder-for-hire plot against Mr Pannun. India set up a high-level inquiry committee after the US first made the allegations in 2023.

## Why it matters

The dispute comes at a delicate moment in relations with Washington. Mr Modi met President Donald Trump at the Quad summit in Manila last week, and the two countries are negotiating a trade agreement. India treats the lawsuit as an attempt to drag its most senior security official into a foreign court over allegations it rejects, while US courts consider private civil suits independently of the government. Mr Doval does not have to answer the summons in person, but if he and Mr Goel do not respond to a validly served suit, the court could eventually proceed without them. No date has been set for the next step in the case.
